title: A Rectangle the World Can Share
bigQuestion: How did a kicking game played many different ways become one set of laws that the whole world shares?

story.title: Two Teams, One Set of Lines
story.kicker: Two teams that speak different languages walk onto the same marked field.
paragraphs: It is 13 July 1930 in Montevideo, Uruguay. The first World Cup has begun. France plays Mexico. The French players speak French. The Mexican players speak Spanish. Few of them can talk to each other.

Yet both teams know the field. They know the goal is eight yards wide. They know the halfway line and the penalty area. They know what the referee's whistle means. The rules are the same for both sides.

Long before, this was not true. Towns in England played rough kicking games with their own customs. Schools each had their own rules. Two teams from different places could argue for an hour before they started.
In 1863, clubs in London began to write one set of laws. Over the next seventy years, those laws crossed seas and borders. By 1930, teams from Europe and the Americas could meet on one shared field.
story.think: What helps two teams play fairly when they cannot talk to each other?

lessons.title: Folk Football in Towns
lessons.mainIdea: For hundreds of years, English towns played rough folk football games with few written rules.
reading: In medieval England, whole towns played *folk football*. A crowd pushed a ball through streets and fields toward a goal. There was no set number of players. Games could last for hours, and people were often hurt.

Rulers did not always like it. In 1314, a proclamation in London, made in the name of King Edward II, banned football in the city. It said the noise and pushing caused trouble. Later kings and towns passed similar bans.

Some old games never stopped. In Ashbourne, in Derbyshire, England, a *Shrovetide* game is still played each year. Hundreds of townspeople take part over two days. The goals are about three miles apart.

words.d: old town games in which crowds moved a ball toward a goal with few written rules
the days just before Lent, when some English towns hold old football games

lessons.title: School Rules and Sheffield
lessons.mainIdea: English schools, a Cambridge group and Sheffield clubs wrote their own football rules before 1863.
reading: In the 1800s, English *public schools* such as Eton, Harrow and Rugby each played football their own way. Some let players carry the ball. Others allowed only kicking. When students went to college, they brought different rules with them.

In 1848, students at Cambridge University wrote a shared set of rules. These are called the Cambridge Rules. They tried to blend the school games so that everyone could play together. No copy of the 1848 rules survives today.

In 1857, Sheffield Football Club formed in northern England. It is often called the oldest football *club* still playing. Its members wrote the Sheffield Rules in 1858. Other clubs in the Sheffield area used them for years.

lessons.title: Thirteen Laws, 1863
lessons.mainIdea: The Football Association published thirteen laws in December 1863, after a split over carrying and hacking.
reading: Ebenezer Cobb Morley was a lawyer and a member of Barnes Football Club. He suggested that London clubs agree on one code. He became the first secretary of the *Football Association*, or FA. He wrote the first draft of its laws.

The clubs argued over two things. One was carrying the ball in the hands. The other was *hacking*, which meant kicking an opponent's shins. The final laws banned both. The Blackheath club disagreed and left the FA.

In December 1863, the FA published its laws. There were thirteen of them. They set the most a field could measure and how a match began. Because they were printed, any club anywhere could read and copy them.

words.d: the group of English clubs formed in 1863 that wrote the first laws of soccer
kicking an opponent's shins, banned by the FA's 1863 laws

lessons.title: Glasgow, 1872
lessons.mainIdea: Scotland and England played the first official international football match in Glasgow on 30 November 1872.
reading: On 30 November 1872, Scotland played England in Partick, near Glasgow. It is counted as the first official *international* match. About four thousand people watched. The score was 0 to 0.

The Scottish side was made up of players from Queen's Park, a Glasgow club. England's players came from many clubs. Both sides played under agreed rules. The match showed that a written code could connect two countries.
That same year, the FA held the first final of its *FA Cup*. The Wanderers beat the Royal Engineers, 1 to 0, in London. Clubs from across England could now enter one contest under one set of laws.

words.d: between two or more nations

lessons.title: Four Nations Make IFAB
lessons.mainIdea: In 1886, the football associations of England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland formed IFAB to guard the Laws of the Game.
reading: By the 1880s, England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland each had a football association. Their laws were close but not always the same. Matches between them sometimes led to arguments. They needed one group to settle the words.

In 1886, the four associations formed the International Football Association Board, called *IFAB*. It meets to decide any change to the *Laws of the Game*. A new law must be approved there before every nation uses it.

FIFA joined IFAB in 1913. Today, FIFA and the four British associations share the votes. IFAB publishes the Laws each year. They are translated into many languages, so referees everywhere read the same rules.

words.d: the International Football Association Board, formed in 1886, which decides changes to soccer's laws

lessons.title: Seven Founders in Paris
lessons.mainIdea: FIFA was founded in Paris on 21 May 1904 by associations from seven European countries.
reading: By 1900, football had spread across Europe. Sailors, students, workers and traders had carried it from Britain. Countries began to play one another. They wanted one body to connect their national associations.

On 21 May 1904, seven members met in Paris to found *FIFA*. They came from France, Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Switzerland. FIFA stands for the French words for International Federation of Association Football.

Robert Guérin, a French journalist, became FIFA's first president. England's FA joined in 1905. FIFA agreed to follow the Laws written by IFAB. A *federation* like FIFA joins many national groups into one.

words.d: the International Federation of Association Football, founded in Paris in 1904
a group that joins many smaller groups under one shared body

lessons.title: Montevideo, 1930
lessons.mainIdea: Uruguay hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930, beating Argentina 4 to 2 in the final.
reading: Uruguay's national team won the Olympic football tournaments of 1924 and 1928. In 1930, the country marked one hundred years since its first constitution. FIFA chose Uruguay to host the first *World Cup*.

Thirteen teams took part. Only four came from Europe, because the trip by ship took weeks. The United States team reached the semifinals. Uruguay built a new stadium in Montevideo, the Estadio Centenario, for the event.
On 30 July 1930, Uruguay played Argentina in the final. Uruguay won 4 to 2. The Centenario was the *host* stadium for the final. Uruguay became the first world champion of men's football.

words.d: FIFA's tournament for national teams, first held in Uruguay in 1930

lessons.title: A Tournament That Grew
lessons.mainIdea: The men's World Cup grew from 13 teams in 1930 to 48 teams in 2026.
reading: After 1930, more countries formed football associations and joined FIFA. Many former colonies in Africa and Asia joined after they became independent. Each new member could try to *qualify*, or earn a place, in the World Cup.
FIFA made the tournament bigger several times. The 1934 World Cup in Italy had 16 teams. The 1982 World Cup in Spain had 24. The 1998 World Cup in France had 32.
The 2026 World Cup is shared by Canada, Mexico and the United States. It has 48 teams, the most ever. More teams give more *nations* a chance to play on the world stage.

words.d: to earn a place in a tournament by winning earlier games

lessons.title: Women Shut Out, Then Welcomed
lessons.mainIdea: The FA banned women's matches from its members' grounds in 1921, lifted the ban in 1971, and FIFA held the first Women's World Cup in 1991.
reading: During World War I, many British women worked in factories. Some formed football teams. Dick, Kerr Ladies, from a factory in Preston, drew very large crowds. In 1920, a match at Everton's ground drew over fifty thousand people.

In December 1921, the FA said football was not suitable for women. It *banned* women's teams from playing on its members' grounds. Women kept playing on other fields, but crowds and money shrank. The ban lasted fifty years.
The FA lifted the ban in 1971. In 1991, FIFA held the first *Women's World Cup*, in China. The United States won. In 1999, the final at the Rose Bowl in California drew over ninety thousand fans.

words.d: not allowed by a rule

lessons.title: IHSA Soccer, 1972 and 1988
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA crowned its first boys soccer state champion in 1972 and its first girls soccer state champion in 1988.
reading: For most of the 1900s, soccer was a small sport in American schools. Football filled the fall in most high schools. Many soccer players learned the game in city clubs instead. Chicago had amateur soccer clubs for many decades, often started by immigrant families.

In 1972, the IHSA held its first boys soccer state *tournament*. That same year Congress passed *Title IX*, a law that says schools that get federal money may not shut people out because of sex. Girls' teams grew in the years after.

The IHSA held its first girls soccer state tournament in 1988, sixteen years after the boys. Today boys play in the fall and girls in the spring. Both use the same Laws of the Game, with some school changes.

words.d: a set of games that ends with a champion

lessons.title: The World Comes to Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: The 1994 World Cup opened at Soldier Field in Chicago, and the Chicago Fire club was founded in 1997.
reading: The United States hosted the men's World Cup in 1994. The opening match was played at Soldier Field in Chicago on 17 June 1994. Germany played Bolivia. Fans came from around the world to one lakefront *stadium*.
When it won the right to host, the United States promised to start a new men's professional league. *Major League Soccer* began play in 1996. It brought pro soccer to many American cities.
The Chicago Fire was founded on 8 October 1997. That date was the 126th anniversary of the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. The club won the MLS Cup in its first season, 1998.
